Of course I'm keeping up to date here to steel some ideas, apologies for just interjecting in your code reviews :)

I'm not sure if I'm hitting a miss here, but I don't think you can be certain the server has received the message when the future completes without problems, is that the intent? Unless netty is doing something magical there, it will just be delivered to the OS buffer if its plain socket stuff. Or am I wrong? that's why I do put everything through a tx log before sending, and only count on the server having received it when the server sends me a message with 'frame completed'. (and thats also why I deduplicate the messages on the other side).

IMHO its great to not have all your eggs in one basket, I'm already benefitting from the ipfw spec trait :)

No it will only guarantee that the message is sent out through the socket.
It is a weaker form of guarantee than what you are doing but with higher
performance since the price is close to zero. It is basically only a
guarantee for network failures. Not that the server is healthy.

I don't know but I think they can coexist and give the user options. WDYT?

It doesn't make any of your work obsolete.

An actor gets a message, instructing it to do some long-running operation. My understanding why this (might) work is the following:
1. The version of a gossip itself cannot be lower than or be in conflict with any of the versions inside its seen table
2. A state (with version) is _candidate for convergence_ if there are no other gossips (and states) circulating that are newer, or in conflict.

So _if a state is candidate_, then we are only interested in tracking its own progress -- we do not care _exactly_ which earlier versions were seen by other nodes (since those states won't converge anyway).

_If a state is not candidate_, then by point (1) it cannot contain information about the progress of the _actual candidate_ (if such state exists), so its seen table will be of no use in case of merges anyway.

Point 1. can be proven inductively. Let assume that all nodes have some state S with a seen table T satisfying (1). A versioned state can be updated in two ways:
- the node itself makes modifications from S resulting in S'. The version of this state v(S') dominates all versions in T since by the induction criterion v(S) >= than every entry of T, and v(S') > v(S). Also the T' table only differs at one place from T -- the node's self entry.
- the node merges S and S' into S'' and T and T' into T''. Since v(S'') > v(S) and v(S'') > v(S'), using the induction criterion (1) on S, T, S', T' it follows that v(S'') is larger than any version in T or T' and the only version that can be larger in T'' than the previous tables is the node's self entry.

Therefore any valid update of a versioned state and its seen table keeps property (1) intact.

Maybe its best that I write the whole issue down. So inside an interpreter all elements are unbuffered, so ASAP and ALAP is exactly the same. The problem comes when you are inside a Processor which has a buffer in front of the internals.

**Issue 1: Making processors that are ASAP and ALAP capable**
- to be able to handle the ASAP case the processor internals needs to be called at ASAP time (out-of-band) to decide whether to progress as ASAP or ALAP
- if ASAP is chosen then the case is simple, just propagate the error
- if ALAP is chosen, then the failure must be "put back on the queue", all elements must be drained, and the failure needs to be handled _again_
- the above reasons made Transformer ugly, because error handling _must_ be split to provide both cases

**Issue 2: ALAP and ASAP don't compose with each other**
If there is a chain: ALAP -> ASAP -> ALAP then basically the ALAP property is already violated because the second processor will drop elements, so the final processor will not see all the elements that the first processor produced before the error.

So in summary:
- inside an interpreter, all chained ops are ALAP and ASAP at the same time, because they are unbuffered
- we decided to make processors ASAP because mixing ALAP and ASAP doesn't really work.

Summarizing my comments to Viktor over Twitter:
- The linked array queues _should_ provide slightly **worse** throughput than the preallocated array queues. This is slightly in the range of a few instructions and is likely to not be noticeable in anything but a very synthetic benchmark.
- The growable MPSC allocates when overflowing the current buffer, this will result in **increased** allocation for a fully expanded queue (consider a capacity of 1024, the default starting array size would be 129, growing to 257, 513 and eventually 1024, so roughly double the allocation. The intermediate arrays have an extra element which is used as a 'next' pointer). This is a transitional effect which only lasts while the queue settles into the correct size. The queue never shrinks. Once the right size is found no further allocation occurs. A subtle side effect of the implementation is that if a consumer **never** reads from the queue, the memory footprint for this queue is the sum of all the intermediate arrays.  This is a trade off for the low initial footprint (which you can set as low as you like, I would have thought 16 is a good place to start).

Given the above we would expect:
- Reduced allocation profile over the linked list implementations.
- Reduced footprint compared to the array backed queue when many actors are present, especially if some are more heavily utilized than others. Footprint should increase when compared to the linked list version, and this should be mitigated (to a certain degree) by setting the initial queue size.

Note that some of the footprint overhead in the JCTools queues is a result of very conservative padding intended for false sharing avoidance.

In view of these expectations I consider the results OK for what they were testing (I'm pleasantly surprised that it's beating the Agrona MPSC queue). You may wish to consider the intended benefit when deciding how suitable (or not) it is to particular scenarios.

With this restriction, I don't think we should see it as a "default" serializer, but a convenient serializer that we will recommend to enable. Must be bound by user to some classes or interfaces. We will not have java serialization enabled by default, so there will be no default serializer (apart for the built in ones, e.g. for String).

I was thinking of adding a marker interface like `akka.serialization.jackson.Jsonable` that was bound by default, but I think it might be better to have it as a more explicit user choice and letting them use their own marker interface (or other classes).

If we decouple 'binding' and 'black/whitelisting', we could bind to Object/Serializable and allow the user to whitelist their whole domain package in configuration? I can imagine some users will dislike having a marker interface.

That was also my initial thought to have a package prefix based whitelist as a complement to the class/subclass/marker based whitelist (which is serialization-bindings), but then I thought it would be better to not have several ways of doing it. At least until we know that it's requested.

I'm not sure it's a bad thing to be explicit about which classes that are to be serializable since there will be pretty common that some classes will require some annotations or specific structure that Jackson understands.

Another aspect of it is that I don't think Java serialization will go away. It's simply too convenient compared to any alternatives. We will not have it enabled by default and strongly recommend against it for production, but for prototyping and early development it makes perfectly sense to me to use Java serialization.

It should be possible to bind both Java serialization and Jackson at the same time. Therefore we can't bind Jackson to java.lang.Object because many classes already implements java.io.Serializable. java.io.Serializable is already taken by Java serialization unless we disallow that binding and require some other marker interface for Java serialization.
